cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK XIII
The sending home;\nthe ship turned to stone; Athena and Odysseus on Ithaca.
So he spoke; they were all hushed in silence,\nheld fast under the spell, through the shadowy halls.
Then Alcinous answered him in turn, and said:
"Odysseus — now that you have come\nto my house with its floor of bronze,
its high roof, I do not think you will be driven wandering
back again as you return, however much you have suffered.
And to each man of you I say this, laying it on you —
you who in my halls forever drink the elders'\nfire-bright wine, and listen to the singer:
clothing for the guest lies packed\nalready in the polished chest,
with gold of intricate work and all the other gifts\nthe counselors of the Phaeacians brought him here.
Come now, let us give him besides\na great tripod and a cauldron,
each man of us; and we in turn will\ngather it back from the people:
it is hard on one man to give\nso freely without repayment."
So spoke Alcinous, and his word pleased them well,\nand they went home to sleep, each man to his own house.
When Dawn appeared, the early-born, with fingers of rose,
they hurried to the ship, carrying\nthe bronze that does honor to a man,
and the sacred strength of Alcinous stowed it well,
going himself through the ship,\nunder the benches, so that it might not
hamper any of the crew at the rowing,\nwhen they leaned to the oars.
Then they went to the house of\nAlcinous and saw to the feast.
For them the sacred strength of Alcinous slaughtered an ox
to Zeus of the black cloud,\nthe son of Cronos, lord of all.
They burned the thigh-cuts and shared the glorious feast,\nrejoicing; and among them sang the godlike singer,
Demodocus, honored among the people. But Odysseus\nkept turning his head toward the blazing sun,
willing it to set: for now his\nwhole heart strained toward home.
As when a man aches for his supper — all day long
his two wine-dark oxen have dragged the\njoint of plow through fallow ground,
and welcome to him is the setting of the sun's light,
the going home to supper,\nand his knees buckle as he walks:
so welcome to Odysseus was the setting of the sun's light.
At once he spoke among the oar-loving Phaeacians,\nand to Alcinous above all he declared his word:
"Lord Alcinous, most renowned among all peoples:
pour the offering, and send me on my\nway unharmed. And yourselves — farewell.
For now all that my own heart wished is brought to pass:
a sending, and gifts of friendship. May the gods of heaven
make them a blessing! And may I come home and find\nmy blameless wife there, with those I love unharmed.
And you who stay: may you be the joy of your wedded wives
and of your children; and may the gods grant prosperity
of every kind, and no evil come\nto dwell among your people."
So he spoke, and they all approved it and urged that\nthe guest be sent home, since he had spoken rightly.
And then the strength of Alcinous said to the herald:
"Pontonous, mix the bowl, and serve out the wine to\nall in the hall, so that with a prayer to father Zeus
we may send the guest to his own fatherland."
So he spoke, and Pontonous mixed the honey-hearted wine
and served it to all in turn; and they poured to the\nblessed gods who hold wide heaven, there where each man
sat. But noble Odysseus rose to his feet\nand set the two-handled cup in Arete's hand,
and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to her:
"Fare well, my queen, through all the years, until old age
comes, and death, which stand over every one of us.
I go now. And you — have joy of this house,\nof your children and your people and Alcinous the king."
So speaking, noble Odysseus stepped across the threshold,
and the strength of Alcinous sent the herald with him\nto lead him to the fast ship and the shore of the sea;
and Arete sent slave-women along with him,\none carrying a fresh-washed mantle and a tunic,
another she sent to bring the close-packed chest,\nand a third carried bread and red wine.
And when they had come down to the ship and the sea,\nthe lordly escorts took it all at once and stowed it
in the hollow ship, all the food and drink;\nand for Odysseus they spread a blanket and a linen sheet
on the half-deck of the hollow ship,\nso that he might sleep
unwaking, at the stern.\nAnd he came aboard himself and lay down
in silence. And they took their\nplaces at the oarlocks, each in
order, and loosed the cable from the pierced stone.
And the moment they leaned back and\ntossed the sea with the oar-blade,
that moment sweet sleep fell upon his eyelids —\nunwaking, sweetest sleep, and most like death.
And the ship — as on the plain a team of four stallions
springs forward all together under the lash's strokes,\nand rearing high they swiftly accomplish their road:
so her stern reared and plunged, and behind her the great
dark-gleaming wave of the loud-roaring sea rushed on.
And she ran sure and steady,\nnever yielding: not even the hawk
could have kept beside her,\nthe falcon, nimblest of winged things.
So running lightly she cut the waves of the sea,\ncarrying a man with counsels like the gods' —
a man who before had suffered pains in plenty, heart-deep,
cutting through wars of men and the grinding waves,
and who now slept without a tremor,\nall he had suffered forgotten.
When the brightest of stars was rising, the one that comes
above all others announcing the light of early-born Dawn,
then the seagoing ship was drawing near the island.
There is a harbor of Phorcys, the old man of the sea,\nin the land of Ithaca: two jutting headlands in it,
sheer on the seaward side but sloping down toward harbor,
which shelter it from the great\nwaves the hard-blowing winds raise
outside; and within, the well-benched ships ride
without a mooring-line,\nonce they have reached anchoring-ground.
At the head of the harbor is a long-leafed olive,\nand near it a lovely cave, full of sea-mist,
sacred to the nymphs that men call Naiads.
In it are mixing-bowls and two-handled jars of\nstone; and there the bees lay up their honey.
And in it are long looms of stone, where the\nnymphs weave cloth of sea-purple, a wonder to see;
and ever-flowing waters. It has two doors:
one toward the North Wind, by which men come down;\nthe other, toward the South, is for the gods: by that way
men do not enter — it is the immortals' road.
In there they rowed, knowing the place of old.\nAnd the ship ran up on the shore a full half of her length,
at speed: such was the drive of the rowers' arms.
And they stepped from the well-benched ship onto dry land,
and first they lifted Odysseus out of the hollow ship,\nlinen sheet and shining blanket and all,
and laid him down on the sand, still mastered by sleep;
and they lifted out the goods that the lordly Phaeacians
had given him for his journey home,\nthrough the grace of great-hearted Athena.
These they set in a heap by the trunk of the olive,\nout of the path, for fear some passer-by
might come and pillage them before Odysseus woke;
and they themselves set off for\nhome again. But the shaker of earth
had not forgotten the threats he had made at the first
against godlike Odysseus;\nand he asked out the design of Zeus:
"Father Zeus, I shall have honor no longer among the\ndeathless gods, when mortals honor me not at all —
the Phaeacians, who are of my very own line.
I said just now that Odysseus\nshould suffer evils in plenty
before he came home — his homecoming itself I never
wholly denied him, once you had\npromised it and bowed your head —
and look: they have carried him\nsleeping over the sea in their fast ship
and set him down in Ithaca, and given him gifts past\nspeaking, bronze and gold in heaps and woven clothing,
more than Odysseus would ever have carried out of Troy
had he come home untouched with\nhis fair share of the spoils."
Then Zeus who gathers the clouds answered him:
"Shame on you, wide-ruling shaker\nof earth — what a thing to say.
The gods do not dishonor you: it would be a hard\nthing to pelt our eldest and best with dishonor.
As for men — if any man,\nyielding to his own force and power,
fails to honor you, vengeance\nis yours, now and always after.
Do as you will: whatever is dear to your heart."
Then Poseidon the earth-shaker answered him:
"I would have done it at once,\nlord of the black cloud, as you say;
but I always shrink before your anger, and I avoid it.
That beautiful ship of the Phaeacians,\ncoming home over the misted sea from her sending —
I will smash her, so that they hold off at last and cease
their escorting of men; and I will pile\na great mountain round their city."
Then Zeus who gathers the clouds answered him:
"Friend — hear how it seems best to my own mind.
When all the people are watching her from the city\nas she drives in, turn her to stone close offshore —
a stone in the likeness of a\nfast ship, so that all mankind
may marvel; and pile the great mountain round their city."
And when Poseidon the earth-shaker heard it,
he went his way to Scheria,\nwhere the Phaeacians are born and bred,
and there he waited. And she\ncame close in, the seagoing ship,
running lightly on. And the shaker of earth came near her,
and turned her to stone, and rooted her to the sea-floor
with one downward stroke of the\nflat of his hand. And he was gone.
And they spoke to one another with winged words,\nthe Phaeacians of the long oars, men famed for ships;
and thus one would say, with a glance at his neighbor:
"Ah me — who has shackled our fast ship on the open sea
as she drove for home —\nin full view, every timber of her?"
So they would say — knowing\nnothing of how it had been done.
And Alcinous addressed them all, and said:
"Ah, then it comes home to me — the old prophecy
of my father, who would tell us that\nPoseidon looked on us with anger
because we are safe escorts of\nall men without distinction.
He said that one day,\nas a beautiful ship of the Phaeacian men
came home over the misted sea from such a sending,
the god would smash her, and pile\na great mountain round our city.
So the old man said. And now it is all being accomplished.
Come then — all of us — do exactly as I say:
cease your escorting of mortals, whoever comes to\nour city hereafter; and to Poseidon let us sacrifice
twelve chosen bulls, in hope he may take pity\nand not pile the long mountain round our city."
So he spoke; and they were afraid,\nand made the bulls ready.
So they were praying to the lord Poseidon,\nthe leaders and counselors of the land of the Phaeacians,
standing around the altar. — And noble Odysseus woke
out of sleep in his own fathers'\nland — and did not know it,
so long had he been gone. For the\ngoddess had poured a mist around him,
Pallas Athena, daughter of Zeus,\nso that she might make him
unknowable to all, and tell him everything through,
lest his wife should know him,\nand his townsmen, and his friends,
before the suitors paid for all their trespass.
And so to their lord all things showed strange —
the long straight paths, the anchorages\nthat take ships from every wind,
the sheer-climbing rocks and the trees in full leaf.
He sprang up and stood, and stared at his own fatherland,\nand then he groaned aloud, and struck both thighs
with the flats of his hands, and spoke in raw lament:
"Ah me — whose country have I come to now? What men's?
Are they violent, savage, without justice,\nor kind to strangers, with hearts that fear the gods?
Where am I to carry all this treasure? Where am I myself
to wander? Would it had stayed\nwith the Phaeacians, all of it,
there where it was — and I had\ncome to some other mighty king,
who would have hosted me kindly\nand sent me on my way home.
As it is, I have nowhere to put it — and I will\nnot leave it here, to fall as plunder to other men.
Shame on them — not righteous through\nand through, then, and not just,
the leaders and counselors of the Phaeacians,\nwho carried me off to a strange country! They said, truly,
they would bring me to clear-skied\nIthaca — and did not do it.
May Zeus of Suppliants pay them for it, who watches\nover all mankind, and punishes whoever goes astray.
But come — let me count my goods and look them over,
in case they carried something\noff with them in the hollow ship."
So speaking he counted up the\nsurpassingly beautiful tripods
and the cauldrons, and the gold,\nand the fine woven clothing —
and missed not one thing. Then,\nmourning for his fatherland,
he crept along the shore of the loud-roaring sea,\ngrieving without pause. And Athena came near him
in the likeness of a young man, a herder of sheep,\ndelicate-skinned, such as the sons of kings are,
a fine-made double cloak hanging from her shoulders,\nsandals under her shining feet, a javelin in her hand.
Odysseus rejoiced at the sight\nof her, and came to meet her,
and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to her:
"Friend — since you are the first I meet in this country,
hail to you! And may you come at me with no evil purpose:
save these things, and save me. To you as to a god\nI pray, and I come to your knees in supplication.
And tell me this too, honestly, so that I may know it:
what land is this? what people? what men are born here?
Is it some clear-skied island — or is it a headland
of the rich-soiled mainland, shelving down into the sea?"
Then the goddess spoke to him again, gray-eyed Athena:
"You are a fool, stranger — or you have come from far\naway — if you ask about this land. It is not so very
nameless as all that: very many men know her,\nboth all who live toward the dawn and the sun
and all who live back westward, toward the misty dark.
Rough she is, truly — no ground for driving horses —\nyet not too poor a land, though no wide one either:
grain grows in her past speaking, and wine as well,\nand the rain never fails her, or the fresh dew;
good pasture she is for goats and cattle; there is timber
of every kind, and watering-places\nthat flow the year round.
And so, stranger, the name of\nIthaca has reached even to Troy —
and that, they say, lies far from this Achaean land."
So she spoke; and much-enduring noble Odysseus was glad,\nrejoicing in the land of his fathers, at the word
of Pallas Athena, daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus.
And lifting his voice he spoke winged words to her —
yet he did not speak the truth:\nhe swallowed the word back down,
forever steering, in his breast, the mind of many profits:
"I heard tell of Ithaca even in wide Crete,\nfar over the sea. And now I have come here myself
with all this treasure —\nand left as much again for my children —
a fugitive: for I killed the dear son of Idomeneus,\nOrsilochus the swift-footed, who in wide Crete
outran all bread-eating men with his quick feet.
He meant to strip me of all my Trojan plunder,\nthe winnings I had suffered pains for, heart-deep,
cutting through wars of men and the grinding waves —\nall because I would not oblige his father and serve
under him at Troy, but led my own command.
So I struck him with my bronze-tipped spear as he came in
from the fields — lay in ambush\nby the road with one companion.
Black night held the sky that night:\nno living soul saw us; I took his life unseen.
And when I had cut him down with the sharp bronze,\nI went straight to a ship of the lordly Phoenicians
and begged their grace, and gave\nthem plunder to content their hearts:
I asked them to take me aboard and set me down at Pylos,\nor at shining Elis, where the Epeians hold power.
But the wind's force beat them off that course —\nmuch against their will: they had no wish to cheat me —
and driven wide, we came here in the night.
We rowed hard into the harbor, and not one of us\nhad a thought of supper, hungry for it as we were:
we simply stepped ashore, all of us,\nand lay down as we landed.
Then sweet sleep came over me, worn out as I was,\nand they lifted my goods out of the hollow ship
and set them down where I myself lay on the sands,\nand boarded, and went off toward well-peopled Sidon —
and I was left behind, my heart aching."
So he spoke; and the goddess smiled, gray-eyed Athena,
and stroked him with her hand —\nand now her body was a woman's,
beautiful and tall, and skilled in glorious handwork —\nand lifting her voice she spoke winged words to him:
"A sharp one he would have to be,\na master-thief, to slip past you
in all your manifold tricks —\neven a god, if one should meet you.
You hard man — shifting-crafted,\nglutton for guile — so not even
here, in your own country,\nwould you leave off the cheating
and the thieving tales that are dear\nto you from the ground of your heart!
But come, no more of this now. We are both old hands\nat profit: you are far the best of all mortal men
in counsel and in words, and I am among all the gods
and famed for cunning and for profit. And yet you did\nnot know Pallas Athena, daughter of Zeus — I who stand
beside you in every labor, always, and keep watch over you,\nand who made you dear to all the Phaeacians.
Now I have come here to weave a design with you,\nand to hide the goods the lordly Phaeacians
gave you for your journey home —\nby my own thought and counsel —
and to tell you all the cares that fate must fill
your well-built house with.\nYou must endure them — there is no choice —
and tell no one, no man and no woman, none of them all,\nthat it is you, come home from your wandering. No:
in silence suffer your many pains,\nand submit to men's violence."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered her:
"Hard it is, goddess, for a mortal\nman who meets you to know you,
however knowing he be:\nfor you take what likeness you will.
This I know well — that you were kind to me once,\nas long as we sons of the Achaeans made war at Troy;
but after we had sacked Priam's steep city,\nand gone to our ships, and a god scattered the Achaeans,
from then on I never saw you,\ndaughter of Zeus — never marked you
setting foot on my ship to beat some grief away from me.
No: I wandered on, always carrying a heart torn open\nin my breast, until the gods released me from evil —
until that day, in the rich land of the Phaeacian men,
when you heartened me with your words,\nand led me to the city yourself.
Now I beg you by your father — for I cannot think I\nhave truly come to clear-skied Ithaca: it is some other
country I am turned loose in, and you are mocking\nme when you tell me this, to lead my wits astray —
tell me: am I really come to my own dear fatherland?"
Then the goddess answered him, gray-eyed Athena:
"Always the same — that mind in your breast!
And that is why I cannot forsake you in your misery:
because you are civil,\nand quick-witted, and steady-souled.
Gladly would any other man, come home from wandering,
have rushed to his hall to see his children and his wife;\nbut you — you have no wish yet to learn or to ask
until you have made trial of your wife besides —\nwho sits as ever in your halls, and always in misery
her nights waste away, and her days, in tears.
I, though — I never doubted it: I knew in my heart\nyou would come home with all your companions lost.
But I had no mind, you see, to fight Poseidon,\nmy father's brother, who set the grudge in his heart,
raging because you blinded his dear son.
Come — I will show you the ground-plan\nof Ithaca, so you will believe.
This is the harbor of Phorcys, the old man of the sea;
and this, at the head of the harbor, the long-leafed olive;\nand near it the lovely cave, full of sea-mist,
sacred to the nymphs that men call Naiads —\nthere is the wide vaulted cavern where you used to offer
the nymphs so many perfect hecatombs; and this\nis the mountain Neriton, clothed in its forest."
So speaking, the goddess scattered\nthe mist — and the land showed plain.
Then much-enduring noble Odysseus rejoiced —\nhe exulted in his own land, and kissed the grain-giving earth,
and at once he prayed to the nymphs, lifting up his hands:
"Nymphs of the springs, daughters of Zeus —\nI told myself I would never see you again. Now take my greeting
and my gentle prayers. And we will\ngive you gifts, as in the old days,
if the daughter of Zeus,\nthe driver of spoils, in her grace
lets me live, and brings my dear son to his manhood."
Then the goddess spoke to him again, gray-eyed Athena:
"Take heart: let none of that weigh on your mind.
Rather let us stow the goods in the\ninnermost hollow of the wondrous
cave, this instant, so that they stay there safe for you;
and let us two take counsel how the best may come about."
So speaking, the goddess plunged into the misty cave,\nsearching along its hiding-holes; and Odysseus
carried everything close in —\nthe gold, the wear-proof bronze,
and the well-made clothing the Phaeacians gave him.
He laid them carefully by; and a stone was set at the\ndoor by Pallas Athena, daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus.
Then the two of them sat down\nat the trunk of the sacred olive
and plotted death for the overweening suitors.
And the goddess began to speak, gray-eyed Athena:
"Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many devices —
consider how you will lay your\nhands on the shameless suitors,
who for three years now have lorded it through your hall,
courting your godlike wife and offering bride-gifts;
and she — grieving without pause\nfor your homecoming, heart-deep,
gives hope to all, and makes promises to every man,\nsending out messages — while her mind wills otherwise."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered her:
"Ah, gods — so I was to have perished by the same\nevil doom as Agamemnon, Atreus' son, in my own halls,
had you not told me each thing rightly,\ngoddess, in its measure.
Come then — weave a design, how I shall pay them back;
and stand beside me yourself, breathing bold fury into me,
as on the day we loosed the shining head-veil of Troy.
Were you to stand by me with that same fire,\ngray-eyes, I would fight three hundred men together —
with you, sovereign goddess,\nwhen you choose in your heart to help me."
Then the goddess answered him, gray-eyed Athena:
"Oh, I will be with you — be sure\nof it — you will not slip my sight
when the hour comes and we are at this work.\nAnd more than one, I think,
of the suitor-men who eat away your living will\nspatter the vast floor with his blood and brains.
But come: I will make you unknowable to every mortal.
I will wither the fine skin on your supple limbs;
I will strip the fair hair from\nyour head; I will wrap you in rags
such that a man would shudder to see a human being wear;\nand I will dim those eyes, so beautiful before,
so that you seem a vile thing to all the suitors —\nand to your wife, and to the son you left in your halls.
And you yourself: go first of all to the swineherd,
the keeper of your pigs —\nwhose heart is loyal to you all the same,
who loves your boy, and steady-hearted Penelope.
You will find him sitting by the\nswine; and they are at pasture
by the Rock of the Raven, at the spring Arethusa,\neating acorns to their hearts' content and drinking
black water — the things that feed the rich fat on swine.
Stay there; sit by him and question him of everything,
while I go on to Sparta, the country of beautiful women,
to summon Telemachus — your own dear son, Odysseus —
who went to wide-dancing-grounded Lacedaemon, to Menelaus,
seeking news of you, whether\nyou were still alive anywhere."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered her:
"Why did you not tell him, then —\nyou whose mind holds everything?
So that he too might wander in misery over the\nbarren sea, while other men eat away his living?"
Then the goddess answered him, gray-eyed Athena:
"Do not let him weigh too heavily on your heart.
I myself was his escort, so that he might win himself
a good report by going there. He sits
at his ease in the house of Atreus' son,\nwith plenty before him.
True — the young men lie in ambush\nfor him with their black ship,
hungry to kill him before he reaches his fathers' land.
But I do not look for that. No:\nsooner will the earth close over
more than one of the suitor-men who eat away your living."
So speaking, Athena touched him with her wand.
She withered the fine skin on his supple limbs;
she stripped the fair hair from his head; and about\nall his limbs she set the skin of an aged old man;
and she dimmed those eyes, so beautiful before,\nand threw about him a foul rag and a tunic —
tattered things, filthy, black with reeking smoke —
and over them she dressed him in\nthe great hide of a swift deer,
worn bald. And she gave him a\nstaff, and a miserable pouch,
ragged full of holes, slung on a rope of twisted cord.
So the two of them, their plot laid, parted. And she
went off to shining Lacedaemon, after the son of Odysseus.
